clue.text: Not just seven-pound molluscs

definitions.note: plural: the word for these cephalopods is unchanged in the plural

indicators.note: 'Not just' asks for seven without the word meaning just, so a word is cut away

parts.note: taken as the word itself
just, as in 'just so', means even
a quid is slang for a pound sterling

explanation.surface: A fishmonger's catch of molluscs that weigh more than seven pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'seven-pound' hides the split: 'Not just' is a removal instruction acting on 'seven', not a comment on the weight.
explanation.definitionFit: These ten-armed cephalopods are molluscs, and the name serves for one or many.

clue.text: Viv from the WI requires junk shop for designer harpsichords

indicators.note: junk suggests the word shop is broken up and thrown into the mix
designer here means rearranged by design, so the letters of harpsichords are reworked

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Women's Institute member needs a junk shop to source harpsichords for a designer.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the answer plus a jumbled SHOP rearranges to HARPSICHORDS. 'WI' looks like the Women's Institute but is the West Indies cricket team.
explanation.definitionFit: Viv Richards was the great batsman and captain of the West Indies cricket side.

clue.text: Artist who rises for long, infinite encore!

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the pieces are read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: to long for is to have a yen

indicators.note: infinite means without end, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: 'More!' is the cry for an encore

explanation.surface: An artist stands up demanding an endless encore from the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: YEN and MOR (MORE without its end, signalled by 'infinite') are read upwards as 'rises' instructs, giving ROM then NEY.
explanation.definitionFit: George Romney was an eighteenth-century English portrait painter.

clue.text: Duke leads salutation for 16's ex-partner

indicators.note: leads puts the duke's letter at the front of the greeting

parts.note: ave is the Latin greeting 'hail'

explanation.surface: A duke heads the greeting given to a former partner.
explanation.walkthrough: Answer 16 is CHAS; Chas and Dave were a London pub-rock duo.
explanation.definitionFit: Dave Peacock was the other half of the singing duo with the entry at 16.

clue.text: Kerry nerd's wound up with inappropriate tip from trainspotter

indicators.note: inappropriate means the wrong tip of the trainspotter replaces the right one: its front end swapped in for its back
wound up, in a down clue, means turned upwards and so read backwards

parts.note: an anorak is a nerdy obsessive; the 's is 'is'

indicators.note: a tip is an end of a word, here its first letter

explanation.surface: A nerd from County Kerry gets wound up after a trainspotter's rude tip.
explanation.walkthrough: Reverse ANORAK to KARONA; the R (trainspotter's end) is replaced by the inappropriate tip, its other end T.
explanation.definitionFit: Kerry Katona is a British pop singer and television personality, so her forename stands for her surname.

clue.text: Is bay having no water around a real find?

indicators.note: around shows the waterless word enclosing the others

parts.note: with no water is dry
taken as written
a cove is a small bay

explanation.surface: A bay left dry by the tide turns out to be a real find.
explanation.definitionFit: A discovery is something found, especially something valuable or surprising.

clue.text: Ambivalent singing from the same hymn sheet?

definitions.meaning: having mixed or uncertain feelings, not committing

definitions.text: singing from the same hymn sheet?
definitions.meaning: read as ..., of equal voice, all singing alike

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the word into EQUI (equal) and VOCAL (voiced); the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Equivocal means open to two interpretations, which is close to ambivalent, undecided.

clue.text: Hume's torn albs it's essential for Jim to wear

definitions.note: possessive: the answer is the first name that belongs to Hume

indicators.note: the vestments wear, so surround, the middle letter
torn albs are ripped apart, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the essential, core letter of the name is its middle

explanation.surface: Cardinal Hume's albs are torn, and Jim must wear them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hume' is Cardinal Basil Hume, Archbishop of Westminster. The albs (priestly vestments) are anagrammed round I.
explanation.definitionFit: Cardinal Hume's Christian name was Basil, so the clue's possessive points to his forename.

clue.text: Spirit of tipsy chef throwing wobbly over dressing

indicators.note: throwing means casting off, so these letters are removed
dressing means the removed letters sit on the outside, clothing the rest

parts.note: taken as written; the letters left after the removal also run unbroken inside these words, but the setter's instructions are the removal, so the plain run is a coincidence of that design

indicators.note: over turns the word back to front

parts.note: to throw a wobbly is to have a fit of temper

explanation.surface: A drunk cook throws a tantrum over the salad dressing, revealing his inner spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'throwing wobbly' looks like a tantrum; FIT, turned 'over' to TIF, is stripped from the outside of TIPSYCHEF, the T and I at the front and F at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Psyche is the soul or spirit, from the Greek word for breath.

clue.text: Behind the scenes? In view, I think

indicators.note: In tells us the letters are tucked inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Someone backstage gives their opinion: in view, I think.
explanation.definitionFit: Something behind the scenes is inside, out of sight; the question mark marks the loose sense.

clue.text: Get comfortably established in ensemble for children's concerts

indicators.note: ensemble means together, so the letters run across the two words joined

explanation.surface: A performer gets settled in an ensemble that plays children's concerts.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensconce oneself is to settle snugly into a place.

clue.text: Barrier provided by English back stopping Rovers star

indicators.note: stopping means plugging a gap, so the star's name goes inside
back sends the abbreviation the wrong way round

parts.note: Roy Race of the comic strip Roy of the Rovers

explanation.surface: An England defender stops a Rovers striker, providing a barrier.
explanation.walkthrough: Roy of the Rovers was a long-running British football comic; 'back' looks like a footballing position but reverses ENG.
explanation.definitionFit: A groyne is a low wall built out into the sea to stop beach erosion, a kind of barrier.

clue.text: Live away from the boundaries of Central American land with a would-be duchess

indicators.note: the word for live is taken away from the edges of the country

parts.note: Belize is a country in Central America
to live is to be

explanation.surface: Someone lives far from the borders of a Central American country with a would-be duchess.
explanation.walkthrough: The removed word is split, one letter taken from each of the country's boundaries rather than from one place.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliza Doolittle in Pygmalion is coached so she can pass as a duchess.

clue.text: Vols contained by taps, always apparently inferior

parts.note: taps in Britain are marked C and H, cold and hot

indicators.note: contained by puts the volumes inside the other pieces

parts.note: ay is an old word for always
V is short for volume, so two volumes are VV

explanation.surface: Books are kept by some taps, which always seem inferior.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chav' is British slang for a brash, lower-class youth, and the adjective is a snobbish put-down.
explanation.definitionFit: Chavvy is a disparaging word for something seen as cheap and low-class, hence inferior.

clue.text: Salts for treating cloth ears!

indicators.note: treating means working on, so the letters are processed into a new order

explanation.surface: A doctor prescribes salts as treatment for someone's deafness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cloth ears' is British slang for someone who does not listen.
explanation.definitionFit: Chlorates are salts of chloric acid.

clue.text: Keeps coming into contact with cold teas

indicators.note: coming into contact means touching, so the two pieces sit side by side

parts.note: to keep something is to have it

explanation.surface: Someone keeps touching cold cups of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Cha is British slang for tea, from the Chinese, so the plural means teas.

clue.text: Strike achieved by Phoenician, perhaps, losing energy

indicators.note: losing means the letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: Phoenicians spoke a Semitic language, so one is an example of a Semite
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: An exhausted Phoenician lands a blow despite flagging.
explanation.definitionFit: To smite is an old word for hitting hard.

clue.text: Old Rosie the worse for wear round back of tavern

indicators.note: round means the scrambled name goes around the letter
drunk and dishevelled, so the name's letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the back of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Old Rosie staggers drunk round the back of the pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Senior means older in years, as in a senior citizen.

clue.text: Bearing drink and bag, Australian left harbour

definitions.meaning: a sweet fortified wine from Portugal
in Australian English, a suitcase or travel bag
the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: Carrying a drink and a bag, an Australian left the harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: Five definitions in a row, disguised as a story about a traveller.
explanation.definitionFit: Each sense is a standard meaning of the same four-letter word, from carriage to wine to the larboard side.

clue.text: Cried uncontrollably, getting mistakenly put in the frame

indicators.note: crying uncontrollably shakes the word up
mistakenly put means put wrongly, so these letters join the mix

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A suspect cried wildly after being wrongly framed for a crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the frame' suggests a suspect, but it means shown in a picture frame.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in the frame of a photograph is shown in it, depicted.

clue.text: Judge recalled failure to get hold of singular poet

indicators.note: getting hold of means grasping, so the letter is held inside
recalled, called back, reverses the word

parts.note: a no-no is a flop or failure
S is the grammar abbreviation for singular

explanation.surface: A judge remembers a poet who failed to grasp the singular.
explanation.definitionFit: Ben Jonson was a seventeenth-century English poet and dramatist.

clue.text: The Listener's influence treated with kid gloves?

indicators.note: what a listener hears is the sound of the words

parts.note: influence is sway, and treated is did

explanation.surface: A listener is handled delicately, as if with kid gloves.
explanation.walkthrough: SWAY plus DID, said together, sounds like the answer. 'Treated with kid gloves' reads as handled tactfully, but the gloves are soft leather.
explanation.definitionFit: Kid gloves have a soft napped finish like suede, so having them is being finished in that leather.

clue.text: For prior future appointment?

parts.note: a prior ranks below an abbot, so his next post would be the office of an abbot

explanation.walkthrough: 'Prior' looks like 'earlier', but it is a monastery's deputy head.
explanation.definitionFit: An abbacy is the office or term of an abbot, the promotion a monastic deputy hopes for.

clue.text: Chucked out my word for 'old hat'?

indicators.note: chucked out means binned, so the exclamation is put into the receptacle

parts.note: to chuck something is to bin it
cor is a British exclamation like 'my word!'

explanation.surface: Someone binned their word for something outdated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old hat' looks like 'outdated' but means a literal old hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A bicorn is a two-cornered cocked hat of the Napoleonic era, a hat from the past.

clue.text: The main track that comes from the Undertones?

definitions.meaning: the lead song on a single, the other being the B-side
a remark spoken in an undertone on stage; the Undertones were also a band

explanation.walkthrough: The Undertones were a Northern Irish punk band, so the second definition reads as music but means a stage whisper.
explanation.definitionFit: A stage remark heard by the audience but not other characters is spoken quietly, in an undertone.

clue.text: Incognito, female victims see and do wrong after a little time

indicators.note: after puts the short time first, followed by the jumble

parts.note: Jan is short for January, a little period of time

indicators.note: wrong means the letters go astray into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Unnamed women victims see and do wrong a little later.
explanation.definitionFit: In US usage this is the placeholder name given to unidentified women, such as unnamed bodies.

clue.text: What may augment veg in difficult voyages?

definitions.text: What may augment veg in difficult voyages?

indicators.note: difficult voyages are rough, so the letters are tossed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A traveller wonders what could supplement their vegetables on hard sea journeys.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the answer plus VEG gives a jumbled VOYAGES.
explanation.definitionFit: The bean is an extra protein that can bulk out a vegetable diet, durable for long trips.

clue.text: Path of this is indisputable

definitions.meaning: the phrase 'of —' means certainly, beyond dispute

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a fill-in: put the answer after 'of' to get a phrase meaning undeniably.
explanation.definitionFit: A course is a route or track, and 'of course' means naturally, without question.

clue.text: Notable ship-launcher only going a fraction of the length

indicators.note: the answer covers just part of the stretch of the following words

explanation.surface: A celebrity launching a ship gets only part of the way down the slipway.
explanation.definitionFit: Helen of Troy had 'the face that launched a thousand ships', in Marlowe's phrase.

clue.text: Intimates bent firms deny I've done the week's work so?

definitions.text: I've done the week's work so?
definitions.meaning: read as 'My, Fri ends!', a sigh of relief at the end of the working week

indicators.note: bent firms are crooked, and crooked letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Close friends at crooked firms deny they have worked the full week.
explanation.walkthrough: Three ways in: the anagram, the plain definition, and a cryptic reading splitting the answer as MY FRI ENDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Intimates are people one is close to, one's friends; the phrase is a common form of address.
